prompt.en: Explain why the sea rises and falls about twice a day, why some days bring a bigger tidal range than others, and why ports and fishers watch the tide.

label.en: The Moon stretches the sea into two bulges and the Earth turns under them, so a place has two high tides a day

level1.en: How many bulges does the Moon make, and what carries a coast through them?

clue.en: The Moon pulls near water most and far water least, so there are two bulges. As the Earth turns, a place is carried through both.

level2Template.en: The Moon makes two bulges, and as the ___ turns a place meets two high tides a day.

label.en: When the Sun, the Earth and the Moon are in a straight line the pulls combine, giving a spring tide with a bigger range

level1.en: On which days of the month is the range biggest, and why?

clue.en: At full moon and new moon the three lie in a straight line, so the pulls combine. At the quarters they act in different directions.

level2Template.en: At full moon and new moon the Sun, the Earth and the Moon are in a straight ___, so the pulls combine into a spring tide.

label.en: Ships need water deeper than their draught, and many fish come closer to shore at high tide

level1.en: What does a big ship need before it can cross a shallow place? What do fish do at high tide?

clue.en: A ship can cross only where the water is deeper than its draught. Many fish move closer to the shore at high tide for food and shelter.

level2Template.en: A ship can cross only where the water is deeper than its ___, and many fish come closer to shore at high tide.

explanation.en: The Moon stretches the sea into two bulges, and the Earth turns under them, so most coasts meet two high tides a day. In a straight line, as at full and new moon, the pulls of the Sun and the Moon combine into a spring tide. Ships need water deeper than their draught, and many fish come closer to shore at high tide.

text.en: A tide begins with the pull of the Moon. It ends with a ship at the harbour mouth and a net in the water.

hints.en: Take the three parts one at a time: the Moon, the Sun, and then the people.
